paper_title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.

sections.content: Robot policy evaluation often relies on binary success signal for task completion. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Robot foundation models have shown strong generalization across tasks, environments, and objects (Black et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). These policies are usually trained with behavior cloning (BC) on successful demonstrations, which treats every successful trajectory as equally desirable regardless of how the task was executed. As result, the learned policy reproduces the mixture of execution behaviors in the data, whether fast or slow, smooth or jerky, and offers no way to steer toward the behavior deployment actually requires. In practice, however, the desired behavior of robot is not defined by task success alone (Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026) and different tasks call for different quality attributes. For example, robot deployed on conveyor line should prioritize execution speed, whereas robot carrying wine glasses on tray must prioritize transport stability. To address this, prior work has proposed quality-controllable policies whose execution behavior can be adjusted along chosen quality axis at inference time (Zhan et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025; Petitbois et al., 2026). However, such policies are trained on static demonstration datasets, which typically cover only bounded quality range and lack the high-performance regimes needed in deployment (e.g., maximum speed or ideal smoothness). Our goal is therefore not only to learn quality-controllable policy, but also to continuously expand its controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations through online data collection and policy updates. In this paper, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), which addresses this limitation of BC by making execution quality an explicit conditioning input (Figure 1). For each demonstration, we measure the target quality attributes with rule-based score functions and quantize the scores Corresponding author: Sinjae Kang (sinjae.kang1@gmail.com). 1 Figure 1: Overview of QCP and iterative hindsight relabeling. Left: QCP controls execution quality at inference time through conditioning on quantized quality tokens. Right: Iterative hindsight relabeling shifts the quality distribution of successful rollouts toward higher quality, expanding the controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations. into discrete quality labels. The policy is then trained to generate actions conditioned on both the observation history and these labels. Rather than averaging over execution behaviors, QCP learns task completion from all successful trajectories while distinguishing how each one was executed. At inference time, the user specifies target label to steer execution behavior, for example, requesting the highest speed label for conveyor operations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond the demonstrations, we pair QCP with iterative hindsight relabeling. At each iteration, we collect rollouts conditioned on the highest quality label, keep the successful ones, relabel them by the quality they actually achieved, and add them to the dataset. We then recompute the quality labels of all trajectories and retrain the policy. As higher-quality rollouts accumulate, the highest label comes to represent progressively higher quality, allowing the policy to reach operating regimes absent from the initial demonstrations. Because quality is measured by rule-based score functions, this loop requires no manual quality annotation. Experiments on Robomimic (Mandlekar et al., 2022) and RoboEval (Wang et al., 2025) show that QCP with iterative hindsight relabeling improves both target quality and task success across iterations, outperforming quality-filtered BC and RL baselines (Mao et al., 2024; Petitbois et al., 2026; Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026). Iterative relabeling pushes the quality distribution well beyond the range of the initial demonstrations, reaching an IQR-normalized Wasserstein distance above 1.5. Beyond single-attribute control, QCP controls multiple attributes jointly, improving six quality attributes simultaneously in RoboEval. Finally, in real-world experiments, controlling execution speed substantially increases throughput in conveyor operations, and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses on tray.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Policy learning with quality control. Prior work studies how to learn different ways of executing task, representing behavioral styles through learned trajectory representations or explicit labels (Petitbois et al., 2025; Zhan et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). Learning requested style, however, can conflict with task performance. SORL addresses this tension by combining trajectory clustering with task advantage weighting (Mao et al., 2024), while SCIQL combines task and style advantages to account for both task performance and style alignment (Petitbois et al., 2026). QCP combines quantized quality conditioning with iterative hindsight relabeling. Our experiments show simultaneous gains in execution quality and task success, demonstrating that this trade-off can be overcome. 2 Online improvement of behavioral quality. Freeform Preference Learning (FPL) learns reward model for the desired quality axes from human comparisons of robot trajectories and trains policies conditioned on the predicted rewards (Torne et al., 2026). This supports online improvement through repeated rollout collection and policy training, but requires additional human comparisons at each round. In text generation, Quark repeatedly samples under the highest reward token, relabels accumulated samples by reward quantiles, and retrains the language model conditioned on the assigned labels (Lu et al., 2022). QCP applies similar loop to robot execution quality, using automatically computed quality labels and accumulated successful trajectories to extend the controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations without additional human annotation.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: In real-world deployment, users often care about quality metrics beyond binary task success, such as execution speed or motion smoothness. To account for these, we propose Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), which adjusts its execution behavior along user-specified quality axes by conditioning on quantized quality levels (Section 3.1). Because demonstration data typically covers only limited range of quality, we extend QCPs controllable quality range through iterative hindsight relabeling, alternating between collecting online rollouts, relabeling trajectories by their achieved quality, and updating the policy (Section 3.2). Figure 1 illustrates the overall framework.

sections.title: ITERATIVE HINDSIGHT RELABELING
sections.content: A policy trained only on demonstrations is largely bounded by the quality present in D. To push beyond this range, we introduce simple iterative pipeline that alternates between rollout collection, hindsight relabeling, and policy updates. The key observation is that rollouts conditioned on the highest bin can exceed the best demonstrations (Figure 4). We attribute this to two factors. First, the label is attached to every action chunk of trajectory, so the policy learns how each stage of the task is executed in the high-quality demonstrations and can recombine these segments into trajectory whose quality exceeds that of any single demonstration. Second, action generation is stochastic, and conditioning on the highest bin of the target quality axis raises the probability that sampled rollout attains higher quality along that axis than the demonstrations. Folding these rollouts into the dataset and recomputing the labels moves the highest bin upward, and retraining on the relabeled data lets the policy produce behavior that the previous policy did not; repeating this expands the controllable quality range over iterations (Section 5.1). Algorithm 1 QCP with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling Require: Demonstrations D, score m, bins, collection rounds. 1: Set D0 D, 1. 2: Label D0 and train πθ0 as in Section 3.1. 3: for = 0, . . . , 1 do 4: 5: 6: Collect rollouts with πθk ( ht, q). Compute m(τ ) for each rollout. Append successful rollouts to Dk to obtain Dk+1. Compute ˆF from scores in Dk+1. Recompute q(τ ) for all τ Dk+1 using Equation 1. Train πθk+1 from scratch on Dk+1 using Equation 3. 7: 8: 9: 10: end for We initialize the dataset as D0 = and train an initial policy πθ0 on it as in Section 3.1. At each iteration k, we execute πθk conditioned on the highest bin = 1 to collect batch of rollouts, and keep only those that succeed at the task.3 Although every rollout is requested at the highest bin, the realized scores vary. We therefore relabel each successful rollout in hindsight by its realized score m(τ ) rather than the requested label, and append it to Dk to obtain Dk+1. We then recompute the quality labels q(τ ) for all trajectories in Dk+1, including the original demonstrations, by applying equation 1 with the empirical CDF taken over Dk+1. As higher-scoring rollouts accumulate, the bin boundaries shift upward, progressively raising the quality represented by the highest bin while the original demonstrations preserve the low-quality range and thus widen the controllable range. Finally, we train πθk+1 on the relabeled Dk+1 as in Section 3.1. Rather than fine-tuning πθk , we reinitialize the policy at every iteration, from random weights for policies trained from scratch and from the pretrained checkpoint for VLAs. This is because relabeling changes which quality range each label refers to, so the label-to-behavior mapping learned in the previous iteration no longer 2For joint control of multiple quality attributes, we compute separate quality label for each attribute, map each label through its own embedding layer, and let the embeddings jointly condition the velocity network. 3We also tried including failed rollouts as additional low-quality data, but found that this degraded performance. 4 matches the new targets and would need to be unlearned.4 We repeat rollout collection, relabeling, and retraining for fixed number of iterations, as summarized in Algorithm 1.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We investigate the performance of QCP with iterative hindsight relabeling by focusing on the following four research questions: (1) Does iterative hindsight relabeling consistently improve the target quality of QCP while maintaining task success? (Section 4.2) (2) Does iterative hindsight relabeling expand the controllable quality range of QCP? (Section 4.3) (3) Can QCP jointly control and improve multiple quality attributes? (Section 4.4) (4) Does our approach remain effective on real-world robot tasks? (Section 4.5)

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Tasks and datasets. Our main simulation experiments use Square and Transport tasks from Robomimic (Mandlekar et al., 2022) and Pack Box and Pick Book tasks from RoboEval (Wang et al., 2025). For Robomimic, we use the Multi-Human (MH) datasets, whose demonstrations are collected by operators of varying proficiency and thus span wide range of execution quality. For RoboEval, we use the demonstration datasets with randomized object positions and orientations. For the real-world experiments in Section 4.5, we use Franka Research 3 arm with the DROID hardware setup (Khazatsky et al., 2024), and collect 400 teleoperated demonstrations for the conveyor task and 50 for the wine-glass transport task to form each tasks initial dataset D0. Baselines. We compare QCP against three groups of baselines. To test whether data accumulation or quality filtering alone can achieve similar gains, we consider BC trained on accumulated successful rollouts (BCacc), and quality-filtered BC using the best 10% of successful trajectories along the target axis (BCfilter).5 To compare against existing methods for learning desired behavioral styles, we evaluate SORL (Mao et al., 2024) and SCIQL (Petitbois et al., 2026), which learn style-conditioned policies through offline RL. Finally, to compare quality conditioning against direct optimization of quality rewards, we evaluate DSRL (Wagenmaker et al., 2025) and EXPO (Dong et al., 2026), which improve flow matching policies with online RL. For both, we add weighted quality reward to the task reward and train them for 720k environment steps, the budget of QCPs 1,800 rollouts (300 per iteration over six iterations) at 400-step limit. Reward settings and interaction budgets are detailed in Appendix C. Quality metrics. On Robomimic, we target execution speed, measured by steps to success, and action smoothness, measured by action jerk. On RoboEval, we target execution speed, measured by completion time, and motion efficiency, measured by total joint path length. We negate or invert qualities for which lower values indicate higher quality to obtain the score m(τ ) used in equation 1. In real-world experiments, we target execution speed, measured by end-effector speed, and transport stability, measured by the end-effector tilt from vertical. Detailed definitions are provided in Appendix A. Training and evaluation. In simulation, we use simple flow matching policy with an MLP backbone, trained for 100k steps on Robomimic and 30k steps on RoboEval with batch size of 1024. In real-world experiments, we fine-tune the π0.5 vision-language-action (VLA) model (Black et al., 2025) for 10 epochs with batch size of 32. These settings are fixed across iterations. We use = 4 quality bins and always condition QCP on the highest bin = 3 during rollout collection.6 At each iteration, we collect 300 rollouts per task and seed in simulation, and in the real world, as 4Reinitialization may also help avoid the loss of plasticity and primacy bias observed when networks are trained continually on growing dataset in deep RL (Nikishin et al., 2022), although we do not study this effect directly. 5In the real-world experiments, BCfilter keeps the best 20% instead, which gives the baseline stronger setting given the small initial datasets (Appendix C). 6Section 5.2 evaluates performance with different numbers of quality bins. 5 Figure 2: Comparison of QCP with BC baselines (BCfilter, BCacc) and behavioral quality learning methods (SORL, SCIQL) across iterations on (a) Robomimic and (b) RoboEval. Each plot shows task success rate against quality metric, with the y-axis oriented so that higher is better. Darker and larger markers correspond to later iterations. QCP improves quality and task success together more effectively than the baselines. Results are averaged over three random seeds. many rollouts as there are demonstrations in the initial dataset D0. These rollouts serve both for evaluation and as training data for the next iteration. Throughout, iteration refers to the policy πθk trained on Dk and to the rollouts it collects. Iteration 0 thus refers to the policy trained on the demonstrations alone, and results at iteration reflect rounds of rollout collection. We report mean quality over successful rollouts and success rate over all rollouts, both averaged across three seeded runs of the full iterative procedure. 4.

sections.title: ITERATIVE IMPROVEMENT OVER QUALITY AND SUCCESS RATE
sections.content: Figure 2 shows execution quality and task success across iterations. Across tasks and quality attributes, QCP improves both target quality and task success, whereas the baselines tend to improve one at the expense of the other, each for different reason. BCacc has no quality signal and improves task success alone. BCfilter and SORL, which train only on trajectories whose label matches the request, discard most of the successful data, at cost in task success. SCIQL keeps all trajectories but weights them by the sum of success advantage and quality advantage, which creates tradeoff between the two (Appendix D). QCP avoids these problems: all successful trajectories are used by conditioning on their quality labels, so even low-quality trajectories contribute to learning task completion, while the requested label selects high-quality behavior at inference. QCP also achieves higher final quality than the flow matching RL baselines DSRL and EXPO  (Table 1)  , even when we assign high weights to their quality rewards.7 We attribute this to the fact that these RL methods for flow matching policies are tuned to consume success signal, and reward along new quality axis is not consumed as effectively. QCP instead provides the quality signal in supervised manner by conditioning the policy on achieved quality labels, achieving high execution quality together with strong task success. 7Appendix compares quality reward weights for DSRL and EXPO. 6 Table 1: QCP versus RL baselines. Results at the final iteration (iteration 5, i.e., after five rounds of rollout collection) are averaged across three random seeds. Higher success rates and lower quality metric values are better. Sq+Speed Sq+Smoothness Tr+Speed Tr+Smoothness Pack+Speed Pack+JPL Book+Speed Book+JPL

sections.title: 4.3 QUALITY CONTROL AND RANGE EXPANSION
sections.content: Quality control across iterations. We first test whether QCP can produce different levels of execution quality on request by evaluating it at each bin in {0, 1, 2, 3} at every iteration (Figure 3). Even the initial policy trained only on demonstrations (iteration 0) follows the requested bins: on Square, for example, requesting the highest bin yields faster execution than the lowest, with mean steps to success of 193.7 at = 3 versus 308.1 at = 0, and the intermediate bins fall in between. We further find that this ordering holds for every attribute at every iteration, even though new data comes only from the highest bin. Iterative relabeling thus raises the quality of the highest bin over iterations while preserving the ability to select different execution behaviors from single policy. Figure 3: Quality achieved at each requested bin across iterations on Robomimic Square. The ordering of the bins is preserved while the whole range moves toward higher quality (arrows). Mean one standard deviation over three seeds. Quality beyond the initial demonstrations. Figure 4 further shows that successful rollout distributions shift beyond the initial demonstration range for Square smoothness and RoboEval joint path length. We quantify the distribution shift using the Wasserstein-1 distance between the initial demonstrations and final successful rollouts, normalized by the interquartile range (IQR) of the initial demonstration scores. This distance exceeds 1.5 for smoothness and joint path length, indicating large shifts from the initial demonstration distribution. For speed, the rollout distribution shifts toward shorter completion times, extending beyond the range observed in the initial demonstrations.8 These results show that online rollout collection and iterative learning enable QCP to expand its capable quality range beyond the initial demonstrations while successfully completing the task. 8In our observations, the fastest rollouts appear to be close to the maximum physically achievable speed in this setup. Figure 4: Quality distributions across iterations. Starting from the initial demonstration distribution, QCP shifts the quality distribution of successful rollouts toward higher quality, extending beyond the initial demonstration range. Arrows point toward higher quality.

sections.title: 4.4 MULTI-ATTRIBUTE QUALITY CONTROL AND IMPROVEMENT
sections.content: We next evaluate whether QCP can control multiple quality attributes in the requested directions and improve them through iterative learning. Bidirectional control of two quality attributes. On Robomimic Square, we train separate QCP policy for each of the four combinations of faster or slower execution and smaller or larger lift amplitude.9 Figure 5 shows that both attributes change in the requested directions over iterations. Across all four combinations, the final policies achieve quality levels close to those of policies trained for each attribute alone, showing that QCP can pursue both objectives together with comparable quality. Figure 5: QCP jointly adjusts execution speed and lift amplitude in the requested directions over iterations. Joint improvement across six attributes. We further evaluate whether QCP can jointly improve up to six quality attributes across four RoboEval tasks (Figure 6). We condition each policy on six quality labels and request the best bin for every attribute during iterative learning (see Appendix for experimental details). The final policies achieve better quality than initial BC and BCacc for most quality attributes across the evaluated tasks. These results suggest that QCP can jointly improve multiple aspects of execution even when single policy is conditioned on up to six quality attributes. Figure 6: Joint improvement of six quality attributes on RoboEval. Final QCP and BCacc policies are compared with initial BC on four tasks. Each axis shows the initial BC score divided by the methods score, so the initial BC polygon lies on the 1 ring and outward indicates better quality. Success rates of initial BC and final QCP are shown above each task. 9Lift amplitude is the difference between the maximum and minimum end-effector height during execution.

sections.title: 4.5 QUALITY CONTROL FOR REAL ROBOT TASKS
sections.content: We evaluate whether controlling execution quality leads to practical gains in real-world robot tasks. We consider two tasks with distinct quality requirements: execution speed for the conveyor task, measured by end-effector speed, and transport stability for the wine-glass task, measured by the trays tilt angle from horizontal (Appendix A). Serving wine. The robot must carry tray holding wine glasses from one table to another without dropping any glass. This task is challenging even for human operators: only 50 of 382 teleoperated attempts (13.1%) succeeded during data collection, as keeping the tray level while moving proved difficult. Conditioning QCP on the highest stability bin reduces the mean tilt angle from 0.0660 rad for BC to 0.0482 rad, 27.0% reduction, while the success rate improves from 30.7% to 42.0% over iterations (Figure 7a). In contrast, BCfilter improves tilt angle and success rate through iteration 1 but degrades at iteration 2, suggesting that retaining lower quality data provides broader coverage needed to sustain task success. Notably, even the initial QCP policy, trained only on demonstrations, already achieves higher success rate than BC. We attribute this to the quality label, which separates stable from unstable executions in the demonstrations so that the policy does not average over them. The final policy succeeds far more often than teleoperation did during data collection. Conveyor belt work. Twenty cans are placed on conveyor belt moving at fixed speed, one every three seconds, and throughput is defined as the number of cans successfully grasped per minute. Achieving high throughput under this fixed schedule requires both fast execution and high success rate. Relative to BC, QCP increases mean end-effector speed from 188.6 to 257.6 mm/s and throughput from 8.2 to 13.0 cans per minute, improvements of 36.6% and 59.3% (Figure 7b). In contrast, BCfilter falls behind QCP in end-effector speed after iteration 0 (217.7 mm/s at iteration 2), and its throughput drops from 8.3 to 6.3 cans per minute, below BC, consistent with the loss of coverage observed in wine serving. The initial QCP policy again already exceeds the throughput of BC, while the final QCP policy surpasses the 173.5 mm/s of human teleoperation, where high-speed control is challenging. Figure 7: Quality control on real robots. QCP achieves higher task success than BC baselines while (a) reducing the tray tilt angle in wine serving and (b) increasing end-effector speed in conveyor work. Values are means over three seeds; error bars and the shaded band around BC denote 1 standard deviation.

sections.title: 5.1 EFFECT OF QUALITY CONDITIONING ON ROLLOUT DISTRIBUTIONS
sections.content: We examine whether the distribution shift in Figure 4 comes from the iterative hindsight relabeling loop or from quality conditioning alone, since conditioned policy might reach rare behaviors simply by sampling more. To separate the two, we spend the same rollout budget in two ways under the best quality bin = 3: 1,800 rollouts from the QCP policy frozen at iteration 0, or 300 rollouts at each of iterations 0 to 5 with retraining in between (Figure 8). The fixed policy reproduces its iteration-0 distribution regardless of sample count, and none of its successful rollouts reaches the 9 Figure 8: Iterative versus fixed policy rollouts at equal sample counts. Figure 9: Quantized labels with 4 to 32 bins versus continuous score conditioning on Square speed. median smoothness of the final iteration. The improvement thus comes from policy updates on the relabeled data, which move the best bin to quality level the previous policy could not produce.

sections.title: 5.2 CONTINUOUS QUALITY SCORES VERSUS QUANTIZED QUALITY LABELS
sections.content: We examine why QCP uses quantized quality labels rather than continuous scores. With four quantile bins, roughly the best quarter of the training trajectories share the best label, giving the policy multiple examples of the requested behavior. Learning from multiple trajectories with the same label can provide more stable training signal than conditioning on score represented by only few examples. The importance of training support is also evident in return conditioning, where Decision Transformer (Chen et al., 2021) and RvS (Emmons et al., 2022) can be unreliable for requests outside the training distribution (Brandfonbrener et al., 2022). On Square, quantized quality labels execute faster than fixed continuous target at every iteration, and four bins also reach higher task success from iteration 1 onward; increasing the number of bins beyond four buys small gain in speed at growing cost in task success (Figure 9). These results support simple quantization as an effective representation for quality control. Experimental details are provided in Appendix F.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented QCP, robot policy that uses quantized quality labels to control individual execution attributes and their combinations at inference time. Iterative hindsight relabeling extends the controllable quality range beyond the initial demonstrations through online rollout collection and policy updates, without additional human annotation. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval show that QCP can improve execution quality and task success while retaining quality control across iterations. Real robot experiments further demonstrate that QCP can be directed to pursue the execution quality desired for given task.

sections.title: B TRAINING AND EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: Policy and optimization. All simulation policies share one architecture and optimizer. The velocity network is an MLP with three layers of width 512 (expansion factor 1, no dropout) and 128-dimensional flow-time embedding; two-layer MLP encodes the observation history of = 2 steps. The quality label is mapped to learned embedding and concatenated with the encoded observation before the velocity network. Policies are trained from scratch at every iteration with AdamW (learning rate 104, weight decay 105, gradient-norm clipping at 10), cosine learning-rate schedule over the training steps, batch size 1024, and an exponential moving average of the weights with rate 0.995. Actions are sampled with nine Euler steps of the learned velocity field. Conditioned on an observation history of = 2 steps, the policy predicts chunk of actions that starts at the first observation of the history; the 1 actions aligned with past observations are discarded, the next actions are executed, and the last one is dropped before replanning. Both choices follow the original implementation of Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023). The quality bins are recomputed as adaptive quartiles of the successful trajectories in the current dataset at every iteration, and rollouts are collected with the best bin requested. Table 2 lists the settings that differ between experiments. Table 2: Per-experiment settings. Steps are gradient steps per iteration. Number of iterations counts iterations including iteration 0, which is trained on the demonstrations alone. The action chunk is written as chunk length / executed steps. Success rates are computed over all rollouts of an evaluation batch. Quality is computed as the mean over the successful rollouts of the batch, first within each seed and then averaged across seeds with equal weight. Real robot experiments. We use Franka Research 3 arm with the DROID hardware and camera setup (Khazatsky et al., 2024). The policy is π0.5 (Black et al., 2025) fine-tuned with its original recipe for 10 epochs with batch size 32 at every iteration, starting from the pretrained checkpoint each time; the quality label is inserted into the language prompt as text. For wine serving, the initial dataset contains the 50 successful episodes among 382 teleoperated attempts; each iteration collects 50 rollouts, and success requires that the tray reaches the target table with no glass fallen. For conveyor work, the initial dataset contains 400 successful grasp segments from 936 teleoperated segments; each iteration collects 20 rollouts of 20 arriving cans, that is 400 segments, with cans arriving at one can every three seconds on belt of fixed speed. Throughput is the success fraction multiplied by the arrival rate of 20 cans per minute. Speed is measured on successful segments and tilt on successful episodes. The quality label requested at collection is the best bin, BCfilter retrains on the best 20% of successful trajectories along the target axis at every iteration, and BC denotes π0.5 fine-tuned on the initial dataset without quality label.

sections.title: C BASELINE DETAILS
sections.content: The BC baselines, SORL, and SCIQL use the network, optimizer, training steps, rollout budget, retraining from scratch, success filter, and seeds of QCP (Appendix B); they differ only in how the training set is formed and in the learning objective. DSRL and EXPO are described separately below. BCacc. BCacc runs the loop of Algorithm 1 without quality label: rollouts are collected by the unconditioned policy, successful ones are appended to the dataset, and plain behavior-cloning policy is retrained on the accumulated set. BCfilter. BCfilter additionally ranks the successful trajectories of the accumulated set (demonstrations included) by the target score at every iteration and keeps the best 10%. At every iteration the filter is applied again to the whole accumulated set, not to the previously filtered set, so the filtered training set grows with the accumulated data rather than shrinking over iterations; the setting does not force the dataset to become smaller. On Robomimic at least 20 trajectories are kept, and on RoboEval the filter is implemented as sampling weight of 0 or 1 without floor. In the real robot experiments the filter keeps the best 20%, because the initial datasets are small (50 episodes for wine serving) and 10% filter would leave too few trajectories to train on. SORL and SCIQL. Both methods proceed in two stages at every iteration. In the first stage, value function is learned with implicit Q-learning (Kostrikov et al., 2022) on chunk-level MDP whose state is the two-step observation history, whose action is the executed action chunk, and whose discount is 0.99 per decision; the task reward is 1 on the chunk in which the task succeeds and 0 otherwise. The value and twin networks are two-layer MLPs of width 256 with layer normalization, trained for 60k steps with Adam (learning rate 3 104, cosine schedule, batch 1024), expectile 0.7, and Polyak averaging with rate 0.005. Advantages are divided by the 99th percentile of their magnitude, and the resulting weights exp(βA) are clipped at 100. In the second stage, the actor is trained. It is our quality-conditioned flow policy with the same network and the same number of gradient steps as QCP (100k on Robomimic, 30k on RoboEval), and the weights from the first stage are used as sampling probabilities over the training samples. The two methods differ in how the weights are formed. SORL (Mao et al., 2024) trains on the samples whose label equals the requested one, weighted by exp(βAr) with Ar the task advantage. SCIQL (Petitbois et al., 2026) relabels every trajectory under each of the four labels, learns style advantage Aλ from the reward 1{z = q(τ )}, and weights samples by exp(β ξ) with ξ = Aλ + σ(Aλ)Ar, as in the original paper: the style advantage is the primary term, and the task advantage counts only for actions that already match the requested style. Both stages are retrained from scratch at every iteration on the accumulated success-filtered set, and rollouts are collected with the best label requested. The main results use β = 3; Appendix reports the other values of β and explains this choice. DSRL and EXPO. Both methods start from frozen flow matching BC policy trained on the demonstrations for 100k steps with the network of Appendix and sampled with nine Euler steps. DSRL (Wagenmaker et al., 2025) learns soft actor-critic policy over the initial noise of that policy (update-to-data ratio 20, discount 0.999, batch 256, learning rate 3 104, twin critics of three layers of width 2048 with layer normalization). EXPO (Dong et al., 2026) learns an edit policy and critic ensemble on top of the frozen policy (eight candidate actions per decision, edit scale 0.1, update-to-data ratio 5, discount 0.99, batch 256, an ensemble of ten critics with the minimum over two), with half of every batch drawn from the frozen policys own 300 initial rollouts. Both act on chunks of 4 actions on Square and 8 elsewhere. 16 The reward has two parts, task reward and quality reward: rt = 1{task succeeds at step t} + λ rq . (6) The task reward is 1 at the step where the task succeeds, and the episode ends there. The quality reward rq is small penalty given at every step, and λ sets how much it counts relative to the task reward. For speed, the penalty is the same at every step, rq = 1/Lref, where Lref is the average length of the demonstrations. Summed over an episode, the quality reward equals minus the episode length divided by Lref, so shorter episode earns higher return and an episode as long as typical demonstration loses about 1. MULTI-QUALITY CONDITIONING EXPERIMENT DETAILS Two-attribute control on Square. Figure 5 uses Square with an 800-step episode limit so that slow executions can complete, ten policies, and three seeds. Each trajectory receives two labels, speed quartile (steps to success) and lift-amplitude quartile (Appendix A), both recomputed on the current dataset at every iteration. Each label is mapped through its own embedding and the two embeddings are concatenated with the encoded observation. separate lineage is trained for each of the four corner commands, namely the lowest or highest speed quartile combined with the lowest or highest lift-amplitude quartile, and every lineage collects its rollouts under its own command. The dashed reference lines in Figure 5 are the extreme iteration means of single-label lineages run with the identical protocol: fastest and slowest speed commands, and lowest and highest lift-amplitude commands. The joint commands reach the two single-label references on both coordinates within few percent, at lower success rate for the slow commands. Six-attribute improvement on RoboEval. Figure 6 uses the state-based policy of Table 2 on the Lift Pot, Stack Two Blocks, Handover, and Valve tasks of RoboEval with the demonstrations of the fixed-position variant, seven policies, 300 rollouts per iteration, and three seeds. Each trajectory receives six quartile labels, one per attribute, each mapped through its own embedding; all six labels are requested at their best bin during collection. The six attributes are chosen per task from the eight RoboEval metrics of Appendix by dropping the two that preliminary eight-attribute run showed to be unaffected by conditioning or to be in conflict with the task  (Table 4)  . The reference policies are the unconditioned BC policy trained on the demonstrations (initial BC) and the unconditioned loop that accumulates its successful rollouts for six iterations (BCacc), both with the same trainer, demonstrations, and seeds. Per-seed values are means over successful rollouts of the evaluation batch and are averaged across seeds. Table 5 lists the values behind the radar plot.

Success rate versus mean end-effector (EEF) displacement per step over successful rollouts on Square and Transport. We compare complete trajectory labels (QCP), segment labels, hybrid labels, and 10% filtered BC over iterations 09; darker points indicate later iterations. Transport 10% filtered BC has no successful rollouts, so its quality values are undefined and omitted. 19 the effect of the iterative hindsight relabeling loop. The frozen variant has the architecture but no further loop iterations, so any additional shift of the iterative variant comes from the loop rather than from conditioning or sampling alone. Statistics are computed over successful rollouts pooled across seeds; per-seed medians agree with the pooled values to within 0.002. The frozen policy has success rate of 54.5% and median action jerk of 0.0335 (interquartile range 0.028 to 0.043) over 2,943 successful rollouts, against 57.0% and 0.0324 at iteration 0 of the loop. By iteration 5 the loop reaches 73.9% and median of 0.0098 (interquartile range 0.0088 to 0.0109). The smoothest frozen rollout has jerk of 0.0171, above the 75th percentile of the iteration-5 distribution. The later iterations therefore produce behavior that the iteration-0 policy does not generate at all, not merely behavior that it generates rarely: the quality-conditioned architecture alone does not reach this range, and the additional shift comes from the iterative hindsight relabeling loop. Quality representation (Section 5.2). This experiment examines how the quality condition should be represented: as quantized label, and if so with how many bins, or as continuous score. Figure 9 compares six variants on the Square speed attribute, all run with the same loop (30k training steps and 300 rollouts per iteration, seven policies, three seeds). Four variants use quantized labels with = 4, 8, 16, or 32 equal-frequency bins, recomputed at every iteration, and always request the best bin; with more bins the requested bin covers smaller share (1/B) of the training data. Two variants use continuous score instead of label: the score is normalized so that the best and worst initial demonstrations map to 0 and 1, this normalization is fixed for the whole loop, and the requested value is set once to the 25th or the 12.5th percentile of the initial demonstrations. Curves are means over seeds and bands are one standard deviation. At iteration 6, the four-, eight-, sixteen-, and thirty-two-bin variants reach 70.3%, 63.2%, 57.7%, and 28.1% success with 139, 120, 116, and 112 steps; the two continuous variants reach 55.0% and 67.0% success with 246 and 209 steps. More bins make executions slightly faster but cost success, sharply so beyond sixteen bins, and neither continuous target matches the bins in speed at any iteration; in success, four bins exceed both continuous targets from iteration 1 onward. Because the continuous variants also use different way of selecting the requested value, this experiment supports quartile labels with per-iteration recomputation as reliable default rather than ruling out continuous conditioning in general.

sections.title: G QUALITY LABELS FOR SHORTER SEGMENTS
sections.content: This experiment tests whether quality label assigned to shorter segments of trajectory is better training signal than one label for the complete trajectory. We compare three labeling options. Trajectory is QCP as used in the main experiments: one label per trajectory. Segment assigns label to every decision step from the score measured in window of 8 steps around it. Hybrid conditions on both the trajectory label and the segment label through two embeddings. segment score depends strongly on the stage of the task (for example, approaching versus inserting), so for the segment labels the quartile boundaries are computed separately within each of ten intervals of normalized trajectory time, and the best quartile is requested at every step. All options run the same loop otherwise. Figure 10 shows the comparison on the end-effector speed attribute for Square and Transport, with 10% filtered BC as reference, over ten iterations with 100k training steps and 300 rollouts per iteration and one seed. At iteration 9 on Square, the trajectory label reaches 84.3% success at 6.08 mm per step, the segment label 48.0% at 4.80, and the hybrid 71.0% at 5.07; on Transport, the trajectory label reaches 13.3% success against 3.7% and 4.0% for the segment and hybrid labels, at similar speeds (5.2 to 5.7 mm per step). The trajectory label therefore gives the largest gains in both success and speed on Square and the highest success on Transport. segment label provides more local signal, but the signal reflects the stage of the task as much as the quality of execution even after the stage-wise normalization, and the policy can improve local score without making progress toward completion. These results support labeling complete trajectories; using finer quality signals may require methods that separate quality from task progress, which we leave to future work.
